title: Responsive Design: One Site, Every Screen

questions.question: The three pillars of responsive web design, as coined by Ethan Marcotte (2010), are:
options: Fluid grids, flexible media, media queries
questions.rationale: Marcotte's formula: layouts and media measured in relative units, plus media queries that adapt layout to the viewport — one document, many layouts.

questions.question: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers:
options: Pretend to be ~980px wide and zoom out, so media queries misfire
questions.rationale: Legacy behaviour lays pages out at ~980 virtual px and scales them down; width=device-width makes CSS pixels match the real screen — the foundation of responsive work.

questions.question: What does clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1vw, 1.25rem) do?
options: Grows fluidly with the viewport but never below 1rem or above 1.25rem
Clamps the element's width, not its font
questions.rationale: clamp(min, ideal, max) gives a smooth, responsive value with hard bounds — ideal for type that scales but never becomes silly.

questions.question: Which layout system is designed for two-dimensional layouts (rows AND columns at once)?
questions.rationale: Grid places items in a 2D matrix (with named areas); flexbox excels along a single axis — toolbars, nav strips, card rows.

questions.question: What makes grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr)) special?
options: It fits as many ≥16rem columns as the width allows with no media queries at all
It creates exactly three columns always
questions.rationale: The browser computes the column count from available space — the layout is inherently responsive; the min(100%, …) guard prevents overflow on tiny screens.

questions.question: In the srcset example, what does sizes="(min-width: 900px) 60vw, 100vw" tell the browser?
options: That on wide viewports the image renders at 60vw (so pick a smaller file), otherwise full width 100vw
questions.rationale: sizes describes the rendered width per condition; armed with it and the candidate files in srcset, the browser downloads the most appropriate one — saving mobile data.

questions.question: 'Mobile-first' CSS practice means:
options: Styling the narrow layout as the base and layering min-width enhancements
Using only px units on phones
questions.rationale: Base styles serve phones; min-width media queries add complexity as space grows — aligning the code's default with the majority of traffic and forcing content prioritisation.

questions.question: Which is a content-driven (rather than device-driven) breakpoint rationale?
options: Target iPhone 14 at 393px because it's popular
Switch to two columns when the text column exceeds ~75 characters and looks stretched
questions.rationale: Device widths change yearly; breakpoints anchored to content behaviour (line length, cramped cards) stay correct as hardware evolves.

questions.question: The minimum comfortable touch target on mobile is roughly:
questions.rationale: Guidelines (Apple, WCAG-derived) recommend about 44×44 px so fingers can hit targets reliably — tiny close buttons are the classic violation.

questions.question: Which media feature respects a user's OS setting in CSS?
questions.rationale: prefers-color-scheme (and prefers-reduced-motion) query user preferences, letting the site honour dark mode and accessibility needs automatically.
